tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove the guide named by short_code; with no short_code, nothing is deleted and the user's guides are listed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Invoke a skill.

Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# Papaya DevSecOps Challenge 1 — Coding Agents for DevSecOps
2	
3	Submission for [DevSecOps Challenge 1](https://github.com/papaya-insurtech/pumpkin/blob/main/Hiring/DevSecOps_Challenges/DevSecOps_Challenge_1.md)
4	(local copy: [work/00-challenge.md](work/00-challenge.md)).

7	> document while writing it; it is not a Papaya sign-off · Updated: 2026-11-09
8	
9	## The problem and the answer
10	
11	Engineering wants Claude Code to talk to AWS directly; Compliance wants nothing to change in
12	production without a named human who reviewed and approved it. The two only disagree about **writes
13	to production**: reads of metadata and all of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence.
14	
15	The answer (the author's proposal): **every prod change is a pull request**, approved by a code
16	owner who is not the author and applied by CI, incidents included. A time-boxed, approved JIT grant,
17	used by a human without an agent, is the only fallback during an incident when the PR path cannot be
18	used. Nobody, human or agent, holds standing prod write or long-lived credentials. Exceptions:
19	k0s/Firebase CI deploy credentials, kept as secrets of a separate `production-k0s` environment (OD1,
20	OD24); the Expo robot token and update-signing key, in a separate `production-mobile` environment
21	(OD40), because Expo has no keyless login from GitHub; and the private keys of the approval-gate and CI-agent GitHub Apps, kept in a secrets store
22	and rotated (G19).
23	
24	| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
25	|---|---|
26	| A free non-prod loop with the agent; read-only prod metadata | Approval **before** apply by a named human ≠ author, enforced by GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent |
27	| One approval (two on process paths and data fixes), same-day ship; incident approval ≤ 15 min, 24/7 | One evidence chain per change, kept 6 years under Object Lock from phase 1; target ≤ 30 min to retrieve it, realistic from phase 2 |
28	| **Costs:** slower incident lane (est. 11–46 min); from phase 2 the agent cannot push, open PRs, run Docker or reach a private registry without a workaround; from phase 1 every `aws`/`pulumi`/`serverless` call asks first, in auto mode too (OD43); raw logs of a service only after its masking lands (deadline: end of phase 2 for claims services); 24/7 approver duty; ≤ 5 days for a new tool | **It does not give:** a technical stop on an agent approving through its engineer's login (deny rules are hygiene, approvals are only flagged); a GitHub login tied to the identity provider (a register does it on Team); prevention of admins editing the gate (logged only) |
29	
30	**Where it falls short** (stated in [framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page)):
31	the JIT fallback meets the approval rule only partly; on GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before
32	apply, so a risk stop holds risky diffs for a second approval; high-risk (L3) changes in deployable
33	code get one approver, from the owners of the path (process paths get two); admins can edit the
34	gate (logged, not prevented); "an agent never approves a PR" rests on policy, training and deny
35	rules that are hygiene, not a technical control; k0s and Firebase are weaker; if the required-check GitHub App is down, every merge is blocked, incident PRs included; whether HIPAA applies is a
36	legal question.

41	|---|---|---|

56	
57	Every claim about a tool carries one: ✅ verified here · 📖 official documentation, with a link or a research row `R x.y` in
58	[work/02-research.md](work/02-research.md) · ⚠️ inference or not verified · [design] my proposal, untested.
59	Nothing was run against Papaya's systems; I had no access to them.
60	
61	## How this was built
62	
63	The repository was written with Claude Code under the same approach it recommends:
64	
65	- [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) set the rules: source markers, no secrets, design only.
66	- From the research step on, each step went to an **independent reviewer subagent** (given the file
67	  and the criteria, not my conclusions) until no HIGH/MEDIUM finding remained or the owner stopped the
68	  rounds; [the log](work/session-log.md) notes fixes that were not re-reviewed. The framing was reviewed with the owner.
69	- **Deviation:** `CLAUDE.md` planned Manual permission mode from session 2, but the VS Code extension
70	  started most working sessions in **auto mode** (transcripts record `permissionMode: "auto"`;
71	  `"default"` only in three short sessions, ✅ grep). Auto mode is allowed by choice (D1), but these
72	  transcripts do not show Manual-mode prompts. Sessions 1–2 (2026-11-08) used the default config profile; later sessions the clean one.
73	- Material choices were taken by the author, called "owner" in the documents (OD1–OD21, listed in the [framework appendix](docs/07-framework-appendix.md#r-authors-design-decisions-od-n-2026-11-09); OD22 onwards are the fixes after an independent review, `work/07-review.md`). They are not Papaya sign-offs; the choices left to Papaya are in [framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page).
74	
75	**Deviation from the agreed form** (framing Q14): there is no Claude Code hook example. The framework
76	defines no specific hook, and hooks fail open unless set to block (framework layer 2); `allowManagedHooksOnly` is in the managed
77	settings example instead (owner decision, [work/05-deliverable-plan.md](work/05-deliverable-plan.md) §5 Q6).
78	
79	## Transcripts
80	
81	All Claude Code sessions for this challenge were run in this repository. The sessions of
82	2026-11-08 up to session 2 used the default profile (`~/.claude`); later sessions use a clean profile (`~/.claude-papaya`, see
83	[work/setup-clean-config.sh](work/setup-clean-config.sh)). Each session is one
84	`<session-id>.jsonl` file plus an optional `<session-id>/` directory holding subagent
85	transcripts and large tool results (📖 [Claude directory reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-directory#cleaned-up-automatically)).
86	They are copied into [transcripts/](transcripts/) before each commit that ends a session. One
87	mechanical redaction is applied: the author's two work email addresses are replaced with
88	`<redacted-work-email>` by [work/redact-emails.py](work/redact-emails.py) (matched by SHA-256;
89	nothing else changes). Git history was rewritten on 2026-11-09 to apply it to every commit.
90	
91	```bash
92	for CFG in ~/.claude ~/.claude-papaya; do
93	  SRC="$CFG/projects/-home-do-hoang-minh-hung-papaya-devsecops-challenge"
94	  [ -d "$SRC" ] && rsync -a --exclude='memory/' --include='*.jsonl' --include='*/' --include='*/**' "$SRC"/ transcripts/
95	done
96	python3 work/redact-emails.py transcripts
97	python3 work/redact-emails.py --check transcripts   # must print "total: 0"
98	```
99	
100	Claude Code deletes local transcripts after `cleanupPeriodDays` (⚠️ from the settings reference as read
101	in an earlier session, not re-checked: default 30 days, minimum 1, cannot be disabled). Both profiles on the machine used for this challenge set it to 365 days.

content.text:
Đã làm xong 5 mục. Tôi chỉ tạo một file là [transcripts/README.md](transcripts/README.md), chưa sửa README, chưa commit gì.

## 1. Đánh giá README (chỉ đề xuất, chưa sửa)

**Điểm tốt:** Đoạn đầu nêu ngay cả hai câu nói và cách giải. Có bảng "Engineering gets / Compliance gets". Có bảng "How to read it" chia theo người đọc, kèm thời gian đọc.

**Đề xuất sửa, xếp theo mức ưu tiên:**
1. **Trả lời thẳng từng câu nói ngay đầu trang.** Hiện người đọc phải tự suy ra từ bảng. Nên thêm 2 dòng ngay dưới tiêu đề:
   - *Engineering:* "Có. Claude Code dùng AWS tự do ở non-prod và đọc metadata ở prod. Muốn ghi vào prod thì agent viết PR."
   - *Compliance:* "Có. Mọi thay đổi prod đều được một người có tên, khác tác giả, duyệt trước khi apply. Việc này do GitHub và AWS IAM ép buộc, nằm ngoài agent. Chỉ JIT fallback là đáp ứng một phần."
2. **Bỏ mã nội bộ ở màn hình đầu** (OD1, OD24, OD40, G19, OD43, L3). Người chấm có 5 phút không giải mã được các mã này. Đoạn ngoại lệ ở [README.md:18-22](README.md#L18-L22) nên gom thành một câu kèm link tới framework §1.
3. **Chia nhỏ hai khối quá dày.** Ô "Costs" ở [README.md:28](README.md#L28) dài khoảng 70 từ. Đoạn "Where it falls short" ở [README.md:31-36](README.md#L31-L36) là một câu dài liệt kê 8 ý. Nên đổi thành bullet, giữ 3–4 ý chính, phần còn lại để link.
4. **Thêm dòng "5 phút"** vào bảng How to read: trang này → executive brief → [diagram 01](diagrams/01-change-workflow.svg). Hiện dòng ngắn nhất cũng mất ~20 phút.
5. **Thêm link còn thiếu:** [work/10-verify.md](work/10-verify.md) (những gì đã kiểm máy móc, là bằng chứng mạnh cho người chấm), `work/07-review.md` (hiện chỉ là code span, chưa phải link) và [transcripts/README.md](transcripts/README.md).
6. **Dời ghi chú "Owner … not a Papaya sign-off"** ở dòng 6–7 xuống mục "How this was built". Đặt ở đầu trang nó gây rối.
7. **Lệnh copy transcript** ở [README.md:93](README.md#L93) đang ghi cứng đường dẫn của máy bạn. Nên tính từ thư mục hiện tại: `SRC="$CFG/projects/$(pwd | tr '/.' '--')"`.

## 2. Các file session

**Cần nhắc bạn:**
- **`d3d5b33a` (session này) chưa được copy.** Copy sau cùng, khi session đã xong.
- **`26fa6806` trong repo thiếu 32 dòng cuối** (1474 so với 1506). Đó là đoạn copy, redact và commit lúc 18:37–18:39, diễn ra sau khi file đã được copy. Chạy lại lệnh copy là đủ.
- **Session review độc lập có đủ:** `dc16c98c` cùng 14 subagent, và các reviewer subagent ở những session khác cũng đủ. Có một điểm nên tự ghi chú: session này chạy trong chính repo, nên đã nạp `CLAUDE.md` có sẵn các quyết định. Sau khi review, việc sửa cũng làm luôn trong session đó. Nghĩa là nó độc lập so với lúc viết bài, nhưng không "mù" hoàn toàn.
- **Chat trên claude.ai không nằm trong `~/.claude*`.** Nếu bạn soạn các prompt dạng `<pasted_content>` trên đó, các đoạn chat ấy không có trong transcripts. Hãy export ra hoặc ghi rõ là không kèm theo.
- Từ 11-08 18:53 đến 11-09 01:17 không có session nào. Nếu khoảng đó bạn có làm ở chỗ khác thì nên ghi lại.

## 3. transcripts/README.md

Đã tạo bảng gồm 14 dòng: session, profile, ngày giờ UTC, mode, số subagent, phase. Cột **Notes** để trống cho bạn điền. Phase được gán từ prompt đầu tiên của từng session và đối chiếu với [work/session-log.md](work/session-log.md). Lệnh rsync không dùng `--delete` nên chạy lại lệnh copy sẽ không xoá file này.

## 4. Kiểm tra toàn repo

| Mục | Kết quả |
|---|---|
| TODO/FIXME/XXX/TBD | ✅ Không còn chỗ nào (đã quét mọi file trừ transcripts) |
| Email | ✅ Ngoài transcripts chỉ có `example.invalid` và `git@github.com`. Trong transcripts: `redact-emails.py --check` ra `total: 0`. Gmail duy nhất là địa chỉ git author của bạn; tôi đã kiểm và trường hợp tưởng là địa chỉ lạ thực ra là ký tự `\n` dính vào. Còn lại là các địa chỉ noreply hoặc địa chỉ công khai (noreply@anthropic.com, aws-security@amazon.com…) và placeholder |
| Tên người | ✅ Chỉ có tên giả trong test (alice, bob, carol…) và team `@example-org/*`. ⚠️ Giới hạn: grep không bắt chắc được mọi tên thật viết tự do |
| Đường dẫn tuyệt đối | Chỉ còn [README.md:93](README.md#L93), có tên bạn (được phép) nhưng gắn với máy cá nhân, xem đề xuất 7 ở trên. Các `~/.claude/…` trong managed settings là nội dung thiết kế. `/Users/alice` nằm trong schema của bên thứ ba |
| ⚠️ trong phần nộp | **Còn khoảng 315 chỗ, và tôi đề nghị giữ lại.** Rule 1 trong `CLAUDE.md` yêu cầu giữ marker trong bài nộp để người chấm thấy chỗ nào chưa kiểm; xoá đi là giấu điều chưa được kiểm. Nếu bạn muốn, tôi có thể kiểm xem các ⚠️ quan trọng đã được đưa vào gaps/open items chưa. Riêng [README.md:100](README.md#L100): ✅ cả hai profile đều có `cleanupPeriodDays: 365`, chỉ phần "mặc định 30 ngày" là chưa kiểm lại docs |

## 5. Đoạn ghi nhận công cụ (bản nháp, chưa chèn)

Đề xuất đặt ở đầu mục "How this was built". Model, loại subagent và skill tôi đã đếm trong transcripts ✅. Câu về claude.ai là placeholder, bạn cần điền cho đúng:

> **Tools.** The work was done in Claude Code, mostly through the VS Code extension, with Claude Opus 5.5 for the main sessions and most subagents (✅ `model` fields in the transcripts). From session 3 the clean profile loaded only my personal DevOps AI kit: rules for safety gates, source markers and secrets, plus skills such as `grill-me` (used for the framing review) and `infra-researcher` subagents (used for documentation research). `<to fill in: what claude.ai chat was used for, e.g. drafting the prompt that opened each phase; those chats are not in the transcripts>`. Each phase opened with a written prompt that named the goal, the output file and where to stop; the agent proposed, I decided, and every choice that changed the deliverable was recorded as an owner decision (OD-n). Research and design steps went to fresh reviewer subagents that got the file and the criteria but not my conclusions, and fixes were applied only after I approved them. Nothing ran against real infrastructure: the agent read documentation, wrote files and ran local checks.

**Bạn cần quyết:** đề xuất README nào được áp dụng, nội dung câu về claude.ai, và có chèn đoạn trên vào không. Sau đó tôi sửa rồi commit cùng [transcripts/README.md](transcripts/README.md). Cuối cùng, nhớ chạy lại lệnh copy, `redact-emails.py` và `--check`, để lấy cả phần đuôi của `26fa6806` lẫn session này.

content.content:
## The question

Engineering: "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly." Compliance: "Nothing changes in production
without a named human who reviewed and approved it." Both are right about what they care about,
and they only collide on one thing: **changing production**. Reading metadata, working in non-prod
and drafting code are not what Compliance's sentence is about. Real customer data has its own,
stricter rules.

## The answer

- **Every production change is a pull request.** A person who owns the changed files, and did not
  write the change, approves it; the pipeline applies it. The same path serves incidents, with an
  on-call approver available around the clock.
- **The agent is never the boundary.** The agent acts with its engineer's access, so the limits sit
  where an agent cannot move them: in AWS permissions and in GitHub's merge rules. Agent settings
  are a second layer.
- **Nobody keeps standing write access to production**, people or agents. The pipeline uses
  short-lived credentials instead of stored keys. The exceptions are named, each with an owner
  and an expiry: deploy credentials for k0s, Firebase and the mobile update channel, and the
  private keys of two small GitHub Apps the design adds.
- **Break-glass exists but is narrow:** when the pull-request path cannot be used during an
  incident, a person gets a one-hour grant, approved by the on-call approver before it starts, and
  types an approved list of commands without an agent. Afterwards the commands are compared with
  the audit log and turned into code.

## What it costs

- **Engineering:** an approver for every production change; a confirmation for each cloud command
  the agent runs; from phase 2, pushing and opening pull requests by hand; raw logs of a service only
  once its logs are masked; a 24/7 rota; a slower incident lane than a direct console fix
  (estimated 11–46 minutes from decision to change, to be measured).
- **Papaya:** the first phase needs about two DevSecOps people and one platform engineer for about
  45 days, because several small tools must be built (the approval check, the break-glass grant,
  the database change path). A GitHub Enterprise upgrade removes part of this work.

## What it does not solve

- Break-glass approves a list of commands, not the applied change.
- An agent could still approve a pull request through its engineer's login; this is forbidden,
  discouraged by settings and flagged, but not technically impossible.
- GitHub administrators can change the merge rules; this is logged, not prevented.
- k0s, Firebase and the mobile update channel have weaker controls than AWS.
- Whether HIPAA applies, and Papaya's legal role for each insurer, are questions for counsel.

=====
## 1. The decision in one page

**Who decided.** This is a proposal by the author of this submission. Where the documents say
"owner" or cite an owner decision (OD-n), that is the author's design decision taken while writing
it, not a sign-off by Papaya. The choices that are Papaya's to make are in the last table below.

**The disagreement is narrower than it looks.** Engineering wants Claude Code to talk to AWS
directly; Compliance wants nothing to change in production without a named person who reviewed and
approved it. Reading metadata and working in non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence. The
conflict is only about **writes to production**, and about real customer data, which has its own
rules (layer 6).

**The answer:**

1. Every production change is a pull request: approved by a person who owns the changed files and
   did not write the change, then applied by the pipeline. Incidents use the same path, with a
   24/7 on-call approver.
2. Only when that path cannot be used during an incident, a person gets a one-hour approved grant
   and types an approved list of commands in a terminal without an agent.
3. Nobody, person or agent, keeps standing write access to production, and the pipeline uses no
   stored cloud keys (a few exceptions, each with an owner and an expiry).

| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
|---|---|
| An agent that works freely in non-prod and reads production metadata | Approval before every production change, by a named person who is not the author, enforced by GitHub and AWS, not by the agent |
| One approval for most changes, same-day shipping, an approver within 15 minutes at night | One evidence record per change, kept six years in locked storage |
| Agent help with incidents, risky-deploy reviews, dependency fixes and audits (§2) | Agent controls as a second layer, never the control of record |
| **Costs:** a slower incident lane; a confirmation for each cloud command; from phase 2, pushing and opening pull requests yourself; raw logs only after masking; night duty | **Not delivered:** a technical stop on an agent approving through its engineer's login; prevention (not just logging) of administrators editing the gate; full approval of the break-glass path, which approves a command list rather than the applied change |

**Decisions Papaya must take** (the design works either way; the recommendation is the author's):

| Decision | Recommendation | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Accept break-glass as partly meeting "approved before applied" | Accept, with its metrics reviewed monthly; Compliance signs | layer 7 |
| One approver for high-risk changes in service code, or two | One, plus the risk stop; two on the files that define the process | layer 3 |
| GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud | Enterprise Cloud in phase 2 if up to about 100 users: identity-linked approvals, prod diff before apply | layer 3 |
| GitHub secret-scanning and code-scanning licences | At least secret scanning with push protection | layer 5 |
| Stored deploy credentials for k0s, Firebase, Expo | Accept with an expiry until keyless login works | layer 5 |
| Staffing of phase 1 | Two DevSecOps people and one platform engineer for about 45 days | rollout plan |
| A 24/7 rota of approvers and responders | Yes; two people awake for a night incident | layer 7 |
| Auto mode on laptops | Allowed, measured, with a switch to turn it off | layer 2 |
| An isolated runtime for the agent (own AWS role and GitHub token, not the engineer's) | Evaluate in the phase-2 pilot; adopt if it restores the agent's push and PRs and costs less than the friction it removes | layer 2 |
| The approval-gate app in phase 1, or a lean first version | Build the app: it prevents; the lean version (GitHub's own rules plus a nightly check of the same rules) only detects, and is acceptable only if Compliance accepts it in writing | rollout plan |
| Whether HIPAA applies; Papaya's role per insurer (controller or processor) | Legal counsel | compliance register |

Sources and detail: the limits in §1a, the research rows in `work/02-research.md` and
`work/09-fix-research.md`, the author's decisions in the [appendix](07-framework-appendix.md).

### 1a. Limits and trade-offs, in detail

The chosen approach is called "A + D2'" in the working notes: option A, the PR path
for every prod change, plus D2', a narrow JIT fallback. The codes used from here on are explained
in "How to read this". Its limits, each argued with its sources in [appendix A](07-framework-appendix.md#a-limits-and-trade-offs-in-detail):

- the fallback meets "approved before applied" only partly (a command list, not the applied
  change), and stays narrow only if most incidents can be written as IaC; layer 7 measures it;
- on GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply; risky prod diffs stop for an owner's look
  at the prod preview instead (layer 3);
- admins can edit the gate, and so can an admin's agent: logged, not prevented;
- "an agent never approves" rests on policy, training and deny rules that are hygiene; "named" means
  a GitHub login that a register maps to a person (layer 1);
- an on-call approver counts for another team's file only in an open incident, checked by the
  approval-gate app; a night incident needs two people awake (layer 3);
- one approver for most high-risk changes; two on the process paths (layer 3);
- k0s and Firebase have weaker controls (G1, G2);
- the approval-gate app blocks every merge when it is down, and is the longest phase-1 item;
- whether HIPAA applies is a legal question.
**Cross-cutting rules:**

1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.

Engineering wants Claude Code to talk to AWS directly; Compliance wants nothing to change in

owner who is not the author and applied by CI, incidents included. A time-boxed, approved JIT grant,

(OD40), because Expo has no keyless login from GitHub; and the private keys of the approval-gate and CI-agent GitHub Apps, kept in a secrets store
and rotated (G19).

|---|---|

The two only disagree about **writes to production**: reads of metadata and all of non-prod are
outside Compliance's sentence.

The answer (the author's proposal): **every prod change is a pull request**, approved by a code
owner who is not the author and applied by CI, incidents included. A time-boxed, approved JIT grant,
used by a human without an agent, is the only fallback during an incident when the PR path cannot be
used. Nobody, human or agent, holds standing prod write or long-lived credentials. The exceptions
are named, each with an owner and an expiry: CI deploy credentials for k0s and Firebase, the Expo
robot token and update-signing key, and the private keys of two GitHub Apps the design adds
([framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page)).

| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
|---|---|
| A free non-prod loop with the agent; read-only prod metadata | Approval **before** apply by a named human ≠ author, enforced by GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent |
| One approval (two on process paths and data fixes), same-day ship; incident approval ≤ 15 min, 24/7 | One evidence chain per change, kept 6 years under Object Lock from phase 1; target ≤ 30 min to retrieve it, realistic from phase 2 |

**What it costs Engineering** (also in the [executive brief](docs/00-executive-brief.md#what-it-costs)):

- a slower incident lane than a console fix: an estimated 11–46 min from decision to change;
- from phase 1, a confirmation for every `aws`, `pulumi` and `serverless` call, in auto mode too;
- from phase 2, the agent cannot push, open pull requests, run Docker or reach a private registry
  without a workaround;
- raw logs of a service only after its masking lands (deadline: end of phase 2 for claims services);
- a 24/7 approver rota, and up to 5 days to get a new tool approved.

- a technical stop on an agent approving through its engineer's login (deny rules are hygiene;
  such approvals are only flagged);
- on GitHub Team, a GitHub login tied to the identity provider (a register maps logins to people);
- prevention of admins editing the gate (it is logged).

[framework §1a](docs/01-framework.md#1a-limits-and-trade-offs-in-detail)):

- the break-glass fallback meets "approved before applied" only partly: it approves a command
  list, not the applied change;
- on GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply, so a risk stop holds risky diffs for a
  second approval;
- if the approval-gate GitHub App is down, every merge is blocked, incident PRs included;
- k0s and Firebase have weaker controls than AWS; whether HIPAA applies is a legal question.

# Papaya DevSecOps Challenge 1 — Coding Agents for DevSecOps

Submission for [DevSecOps Challenge 1](https://github.com/papaya-insurtech/pumpkin/blob/main/Hiring/DevSecOps_Challenges/DevSecOps_Challenge_1.md)
(local copy: [work/00-challenge.md](work/00-challenge.md)) · Status: complete · Updated: 2026-11-09

## The problem and the answer

- **Engineering: "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly."** Yes: freely in non-prod, and in prod
  for reading metadata. A change to prod is a pull request, which the agent can help write.
- **Compliance: "Nothing changes in production without a named human who reviewed and approved
  it."** Yes: every prod change is approved before it is applied, by a named person who is not its
  author, enforced by GitHub and AWS IAM outside the agent. One partial exception: the break-glass
  fallback during an incident (below).

The two only disagree about **writes to production**: reads of metadata and all of non-prod are
outside Compliance's sentence.

The answer (the author's proposal): **every prod change is a pull request**, approved by a code
owner who is not the author and applied by CI, incidents included. A time-boxed, approved JIT grant,
used by a human without an agent, is the only fallback during an incident when the PR path cannot be
used. Nobody, human or agent, holds standing prod write or long-lived credentials. The exceptions
are named, each with an owner and an expiry: CI deploy credentials for k0s and Firebase, the Expo
robot token and update-signing key, and the private keys of two GitHub Apps the design adds
([framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page)).

| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
|---|---|
| A free non-prod loop with the agent; read-only prod metadata | Approval **before** apply by a named human ≠ author, enforced by GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent |
| One approval (two on process paths and data fixes), same-day ship; incident approval ≤ 15 min, 24/7 | One evidence chain per change, kept 6 years under Object Lock from phase 1; target ≤ 30 min to retrieve it, realistic from phase 2 |

**What it costs Engineering** (also in the [executive brief](docs/00-executive-brief.md#what-it-costs)):

- a slower incident lane than a console fix: an estimated 11–46 min from decision to change;
- from phase 1, a confirmation for every `aws`, `pulumi` and `serverless` call, in auto mode too;
- from phase 2, the agent cannot push, open pull requests, run Docker or reach a private registry
  without a workaround;
- raw logs of a service only after its masking lands (deadline: end of phase 2 for claims services);
- a 24/7 approver rota, and up to 5 days to get a new tool approved.

**What it does not give Compliance:**

- a technical stop on an agent approving through its engineer's login (deny rules are hygiene;
  such approvals are only flagged);
- on GitHub Team, a GitHub login tied to the identity provider (a register maps logins to people);
- prevention of admins editing the gate (it is logged).

**Where else it falls short** (all limits, with sources, in
[framework §1a](docs/01-framework.md#1a-limits-and-trade-offs-in-detail)):

- the break-glass fallback meets "approved before applied" only partly: it approves a command
  list, not the applied change;
- on GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply, so a risk stop holds risky diffs for a
  second approval;
- if the approval-gate GitHub App is down, every merge is blocked, incident PRs included;
- k0s and Firebase have weaker controls than AWS; whether HIPAA applies is a legal question.

## How to read it

| You are | Read | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Short on time | This page and the [change workflow diagram](diagrams/01-change-workflow.svg) | ~5 min |
| Decision panel | [Executive brief](docs/00-executive-brief.md) (plain language, no codes), [framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page) with the decisions Papaya must take, [diagrams](diagrams/README.md) | ~20 min |
| Compliance | [Compliance register](docs/04-compliance-mapping.md), [threat model](docs/05-threat-model.md), [problem → control map](docs/06-problem-control-map.md) | ~45 min |
| Engineer | [Engineer guide](docs/02-engineer-guide.md), [framework §2](docs/01-framework.md#2-agent-assisted-devsecops-workflows) (how the agents are used), [examples](examples/README.md), framework layers 1–3 | ~45 min |

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| [docs/](docs/) | Executive brief; framework (the decision, agent-assisted workflows, 8 layers: principle, Papaya's stack, audit evidence, cost/value); guide, rollout, register, threat model, map, [framework appendix](docs/07-framework-appendix.md) (detail, gaps, the author's decisions), [ADRs](docs/adr/README.md) |
| [examples/](examples/README.md) | Ruleset, CODEOWNERS, workflows, a runnable risk stop, IAM/OIDC/SCP, managed settings, plugin marketplace, policy pack; each with a local check and what it does **not** prove |
| [diagrams/](diagrams/README.md) | Change workflow, trust boundaries, incident lane |
| [work/](work/) | Working notes and decision log (Vietnamese, with English summaries), including the [independent review](work/07-review.md) and the [verify report](work/10-verify.md) |
| [transcripts/](transcripts/) | Complete Claude Code session files, raw except the redaction of two work email addresses (see below); [session index](transcripts/README.md) |
| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) | The rules the agent followed in this repository |

## Evidence markers

Every claim about a tool carries one: ✅ verified here · 📖 official documentation, with a link or a research row `R x.y` in
[work/02-research.md](work/02-research.md) · ⚠️ inference or not verified · [design] my proposal, untested.
Nothing was run against Papaya's systems; I had no access to them.

## How this was built

The repository was written with Claude Code under the same approach it recommends:

- [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) set the rules: source markers, no secrets, design only.
- From the research step on, each step went to an **independent reviewer subagent** (given the file
  and the criteria, not my conclusions) until no HIGH/MEDIUM finding remained or the owner stopped the
  rounds; [the log](work/session-log.md) notes fixes that were not re-reviewed. The framing was reviewed with the owner.
- **Deviation:** `CLAUDE.md` planned Manual permission mode from session 2, but the VS Code extension
  started most working sessions in **auto mode** (transcripts record `permissionMode: "auto"`;
  `"default"` only in three short sessions, ✅ grep). Auto mode is allowed by choice (D1), but these
  transcripts do not show Manual-mode prompts. Sessions 1–2 (2026-11-08) used the default config profile; later sessions the clean one.
- Material choices were taken by the author, called "owner" in the documents (OD1–OD21, listed in the [framework appendix](docs/07-framework-appendix.md#r-authors-design-decisions-od-n-2026-11-09); OD22 onwards are the fixes after an independent review, `work/07-review.md`). They are not Papaya sign-offs; the choices left to Papaya are in [framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page).

**Deviation from the agreed form** (framing Q14): there is no Claude Code hook example. The framework
defines no specific hook, and hooks fail open unless set to block (framework layer 2); `allowManagedHooksOnly` is in the managed
settings example instead (owner decision, [work/05-deliverable-plan.md](work/05-deliverable-plan.md) §5 Q6).

## Transcripts

All Claude Code sessions for this challenge were run in this repository. The sessions of
2026-11-08 up to session 2 used the default profile (`~/.claude`); later sessions use a clean profile (`~/.claude-papaya`, see
[work/setup-clean-config.sh](work/setup-clean-config.sh)). Each session is one
`<session-id>.jsonl` file plus an optional `<session-id>/` directory holding subagent
transcripts and large tool results (📖 [Claude directory reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-directory#cleaned-up-automatically)).
They are copied into [transcripts/](transcripts/) before each commit that ends a session. One
mechanical redaction is applied: the author's two work email addresses are replaced with
`<redacted-work-email>` by [work/redact-emails.py](work/redact-emails.py) (matched by SHA-256;
nothing else changes). Git history was rewritten on 2026-11-09 to apply it to every commit.

```bash
for CFG in ~/.claude ~/.claude-papaya; do
  SRC="$CFG/projects/-home-do-hoang-minh-hung-papaya-devsecops-challenge"
  [ -d "$SRC" ] && rsync -a --exclude='memory/' --include='*.jsonl' --include='*/' --include='*/**' "$SRC"/ transcripts/
done
python3 work/redact-emails.py transcripts
python3 work/redact-emails.py --check transcripts   # must print "total: 0"
```

Claude Code deletes local transcripts after `cleanupPeriodDays` (⚠️ from the settings reference as read
in an earlier session, not re-checked: default 30 days, minimum 1, cannot be disabled). Both profiles on the machine used for this challenge set it to 365 days.

content.text:
Tôi đã sửa README theo cả 7 đề xuất và chèn đoạn Tools. Chưa commit.

**Phần đầu README**
- Ngay dưới tiêu đề là hai bullet trích nguyên văn câu nói của Engineering và Compliance, mỗi câu kèm câu trả lời trực tiếp.
- Đã bỏ các mã OD1, OD24, OD40, G19, OD43, L3 khỏi màn hình đầu. Đoạn ngoại lệ gom thành một câu: "named, each with an owner and an expiry". Cách nói này lấy từ executive brief và framework §1.
- Bảng chỉ còn hai dòng "gets". Phần chi phí và hạn chế chuyển thành ba danh sách bullet ngắn:
  - **What it costs Engineering:** giữ đủ 6 mục, link tới mục "What it costs" của executive brief.
  - **What it does not give Compliance:** 3 mục.
  - **Where else it falls short:** 4 dòng, link tới [framework §1a](docs/01-framework.md#1a-limits-and-trade-offs-in-detail). Framework §1 không chứa đủ các mục này, chỉ §1a có, nên tôi đổi link cho đúng.
- Bảng How to read có thêm dòng "Short on time, ~5 min": đọc trang này và sơ đồ change workflow.

**Các sửa còn lại**
- Ghi chú "Owner … not a Papaya sign-off" đã dời xuống mục "How this was built".
- Thêm link tới [work/07-review.md](work/07-review.md), [work/10-verify.md](work/10-verify.md) và [transcripts/README.md](transcripts/README.md).
- Lệnh copy transcript giờ tính đường dẫn bằng `$(pwd | tr '/.' '--')`. Chạy thử từ thư mục gốc repo cho ra đúng tên thư mục cũ.

**Đoạn Tools, có hai chỗ khác bản nháp**
- **Câu về claude.ai:** bạn chưa điền mục đích, nên tôi viết trung tính: "I also used claude.ai chat outside Claude Code; those conversations are not part of the transcripts." Nếu muốn ghi rõ bạn dùng nó để làm gì, cho tôi một câu.
- **Câu "fixes were applied only after I approved them" trong bản nháp là sai.** [work/session-log.md:612](work/session-log.md#L612) ghi rằng lỗi về sự thật được sửa ngay, chỉ những sửa đổi thiết kế mới chờ owner quyết. Tôi đã viết lại đúng như vậy.
- Các chi tiết khác đều đã kiểm trong transcripts: model là Opus 5.5, `grill-me` dùng ở session `28544ac2`, `infra-researcher` dùng ở session `dc16c98c`.

**Kiểm tra:** Link và anchor trong README.md và transcripts/README.md không có cái nào hỏng (script tự viết, kiểm theo cách GitHub tạo anchor). README dài thêm, từ 1183 lên 1473 từ, chủ yếu do đoạn Tools. Phần đầu trang thì dễ đọc lướt hơn trước.

Tôi chưa cho subagent độc lập review README. `CLAUDE.md` chỉ bắt buộc review cho bước research và thiết kế. Nếu bạn muốn một lượt đọc bằng con mắt người chấm thì tôi chạy.

**Bước tiếp theo:**
1. Bạn có muốn tôi commit README.md và transcripts/README.md ngay không?
2. Cuối session, chạy lại lệnh copy, rồi `python3 work/redact-emails.py transcripts`, rồi `--check` (phải ra `total: 0`). Lệnh copy sẽ lấy phần đuôi còn thiếu của `26fa6806` và cả session này (`d3d5b33a`).
